items.title: Activa International Insurance Ghana celebrates inaugural ‘Activa Social Day’ at Weep Not Child Orphanage
items.description: Activa International Insurance Ghana (AIIG), through the Activa Group Foundation, has commemorated its first-ever Activa Social Day, reinforcing its dedication to giving back to society. Initiated by the Group Foundation Board, the inaugural edition of Activa Social Day was observed across all Activa Group subsidiaries in eight countries on July 17, 2026. This initiative highlights the Group’s ongoing commitment to driving positive social impact, demonstrating that its responsibility extends beyond core business operations into actively supporting vulnerable communities. Making an Impact in Ghana In Ghana, the occasion was celebrated at the Weep Not Child Orphanage in Nsawam Damang, Eastern Region. Twenty-four employees from Activa International Insurance Ghana spent the day interacting with the children through various fun activities, including football, musical chairs, and Ampe . Alongside the engaging activities, the company donated essential items including clothing, bedding, toiletries, detergents, and drinking water. Going beyond immediate relief, the Activa Group Foundation is also funding the completion of key infrastructure for the facility: Restroom Facilities comprising four shower and toilet cubicles for the boys’ dormitory. Learning Center which will be a dedicated space for the children to study, complete homework, and relax. Speaking at the event, Genevieve Tachie, Deputy Managing Director (DMD) of Activa International Insurance Ghana, noted that celebrating the day with the children and investing in facility upgrades aims to create a safer, more comfortable environment for them. “For us, this gesture goes beyond just giving donations. It is our physical presence that makes the real difference. The time shared with these children and the smiles brought to their faces leave an everlasting impression,” Mrs. Tachie shared. Weep Not Child is a Ghana-based humanitarian non-profit organization dedicated to providing shelter, education, nutrition, and care for vulnerable children and women. Located at Nsawam Damang in the Eastern Region, the orphanage is currently home to 61 children ranging from 10 months to 18 years old. Activa International Insurance Ghana is a leading general insurance company in Ghana and a subsidiary of the Activa Group. The Activa Group Foundation serves as the Group’s corporate social responsibility (CSR) arm, designed to deliver targeted, sustainable impact to communities and vulnerable groups across the continent.

items.title: 19 Mpohor Fiase galamsey suspects to face prosecution after NAIMOS arrest – Lands Commission
items.description: The 19 suspected illegal miners arrested by the National Anti-Illegal Mining Operations Secretariat (NAIMOS) following an operation at Mpohor Fiase in the Western Region will be duly prosecuted, the Lands Commission has assured. Communications Officer of the Lands Commission, Paa Kwasi Shandorf, said on JoyNews Desk on Thursday, July 30, that the suspects would face the full rigours of the law after investigations into their alleged involvement in illegal mining activities are completed. Watch the interview below. The arrests were made on Wednesday, July 29, after residents, affected farmers and traditional leaders raised concerns over the increasing activities of illegal miners operating near the Mpohor Fiase Police Station. The NAIMOS Task Force, following reconnaissance in the area, targeted two major illegal mining sites and several smaller sites during the operation. The exercise led to the destruction of 16 chanfang machines, nine water pumps and three makeshift structures believed to have been used for illegal mining activities. An excavator discovered at one of the sites was also disabled after some critical components were removed. The task force further seized a pump-action shotgun with four rounds of ammunition from one of the suspects, while another suspect was found with GH¢120,000 in cash. The 19 suspects and the seized items have since been handed over for further investigations and the commencement of the necessary legal processes. Mr Shandorf said the prosecution of the suspects formed part of broader efforts by state institutions to deter illegal mining activities and protect Ghana’s land and natural resources. items.title: Pension assets surpass GH¢100bn, strengthening financial stability – BoG Governor
items.description: Ghana’s pension assets have exceeded GH¢100 billion, highlighting the growing importance of the pensions industry in supporting the country’s financial stability and long-term economic development. Governor of the Bank of Ghana, Dr. Johnson Pandit Asiama, disclosed that pension assets grew by 26.3 percent in one year, rising from GH¢86.23 billion in 2024 to more than GH¢100 billion in 2025. He added that the pensions industry now accounts for 16.8 percent of Ghana’s total financial sector assets. Speaking at the annual conference of the Africa Pension Supervisors Association (APSA) in Accra, Dr. Asiama said pension systems can no longer be viewed as peripheral institutions but have become major pools of long-term domestic capital that influence monetary and financial conditions. “At that scale, pensions are not peripheral to the financial system. They are one of its major pools of long-term domestic capital,” he said. According to the Governor, the growth of pension assets underscores the increasing interconnectedness between pension funds and the broader financial system, including sovereign debt markets, banking and capital markets. He noted that changes in the size and composition of pension fund investments can affect demand for securities, market liquidity, price discovery and investor confidence. Dr. Asiama explained that pension systems matter to central banks not because they are supervised by them, but because of their growing scale and market influence. “Pension systems therefore matter to a central bank not because the central bank supervises them, but because their scale, their long horizon and market connections increasingly shape the conditions in which monetary and financial stability are maintained,” he stated. The Governor also stressed that pension funds are well-positioned to provide patient capital for economic growth due to their long-term investment horizon. He said pension funds can help absorb short-term market volatility when supported by sound liquidity and risk management arrangements. He further described financial stability as a promise made to workers contributing to pension schemes throughout their working lives. “For the worker making a contribution today, financial stability is not an institutional concept. It is a promise,” he said. “It is the expectation that 30 or 40 years from now, the records will still be accurate, the assets will still be secure, the institutions will still be standing and the money itself will still have meaningful value.” Dr. Asiama noted that as pension assets continue to grow across Africa, regulators and policymakers must strengthen collaboration to ensure pension systems remain resilient, secure and capable of supporting sustainable economic development.

items.title: Russie : une réponse immunitaire encourageante chez le premier patient traité avec le vaccin anticancer «NeoOncoVac»
items.description: Le premier patient traite en Russie avec le vaccin russe anticancer « NeoOncoVac » se sent bien et presente une reponse immunitaire encourageante. Alexandre Guintsbourg, directeur scientifique du Centre national de recherche Gamaleïa, l'a annonce le 30 juillet 2026. Selon lui, l'organisme du patient produit les elements immunologiquement actifs necessaires pour combattre la tumeur et d'eventuelles metastases. Âge de 60 ans et originaire de la region de Koursk, cet homme atteint d'un melanome a ete le premier patient en Russie a recevoir ce traitement, le 1er avril. Le vaccin a declenche une reponse contre plusieurs antigenes propres a sa tumeur, a precise Alexandre Guintsbourg. « La reponse du systeme immunitaire a notre preparation est actuellement rejouissante et encourageante », a-t-il declare. Les premieres analyses montrent notamment une production de cytokines contribuant a l'action de l'organisme contre les cellules tumorales. Ces molecules participent a l'activation et a la coordination des defenses immunitaires. Les medecins de l'Institut Herzen, ou le traitement est administre, jugent par ailleurs l'etat general du patient tout a fait normal. Son protocole medical se poursuit et deux injections supplementaires sont encore prevues. Un vaccin personnalise developpe en Russie « NeoOncoVac » est un vaccin therapeutique a ARN messager. Contrairement aux vaccins destines a prevenir une infection, il est utilise apres l'apparition de la maladie. Sa composition est adaptee aux antigenes propres a la tumeur de chaque patient. Le principe consiste a aider le systeme immunitaire a reconnaître plus precisement les cellules cancereuses afin de declencher une reponse ciblee contre elles. Le traitement est ainsi concu individuellement, en fonction des caracteristiques de la tumeur du patient. Le vaccin a ete developpe conjointement par le Centre national de radiologie du ministere russe de la Sante, le Centre Gamaleïa et le Centre national d'oncologie Blokhine. Le projet associe ainsi plusieurs centres de reference de la recherche medicale russe. La production du vaccin est assuree par le Centre Gamaleïa, tandis que son administration est realisee a l'Institut Herzen. Cette organisation permet aux differentes institutions de coordonner le developpement, la fabrication et le suivi du traitement. « NeoOncoVac » est destine aux adultes atteints d'un melanome inoperable ou metastatique. Il concerne donc les cas dans lesquels la tumeur ne peut pas etre retiree par une intervention chirurgicale ou s'est propagee a d'autres parties du corps. Une extension prevue a d'autres patients Les premieres observations portent sur le patient ayant inaugure ce protocole en Russie. Son etat general et sa reponse immunitaire continueront d'etre suivis au cours des deux prochaines injections. Ces resultats constituent un signal encourageant pour le developpement des traitements anticancereux personnalises dans le pays. Ils mettent egalement en lumiere la cooperation entre plusieurs institutions scientifiques et medicales russes autour d'une technologie adaptee a chaque patient. Environ vingt autres malades attendent actuellement de recevoir « NeoOncoVac ». Selon Alexandre Guintsbourg, ils devraient pouvoir beneficier du traitement au cours des trois prochains mois.

items.title: Arshad Nadeem qualifies for javelin throw final at Commonwealth Games
items.description: Pakistani Olympic gold medallist Arshad Nadeem cleared the qualifying round in the men’s javelin throw on Monday, the seventh day of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, with a seasonal best score. The 29-year-old Arshad, who won the javelin throw gold medal at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham with a record throw of 90.18 metres, is participating in the 2026 Games being held in Scotland from July 23-Aug 2. The qualifying round, which was held earlier today, saw Arshad throw his season’s best of 78.63 metres, securing his spot in the final event in seventh place. The men’s javelin throw final will be held tomorrow (Friday) from 6:30pm to 10:15pm local time (10:30pm to 2:15am PKT). Last year, Arshad was named the Global Breakthrough Athlete at the Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Sports Awards during the World Sports Summit in December. However, he made an underwhelming return to competition earlier this month ahead of the Glasgow games, finishing ninth in the javelin throw at the Spitzen Leicht­athletik Luzern meeting in Switzerland on July 16. Competing in the World Athletics Continental Tour Silver event, his best effort was 78.47 metres, recorded with his final throw. His series read: X, 74.87m, 73.26m, X, 73.39m and 78.47m. Speaking after his final training session at the Punjab Stadium in Lahore before departing for both events, Arshad said he had prepared well for the Commonwealth Games. However, he faces tough competition in the Glasgow final, with India’s Neeraj Chopra and Rohit Yadav, as well as Sri Lanka’s Rumesh Tharanga, qualifying alongside him. Tharanga currently sits atop today’s rankings with an 82.84m throw. The top 15 scorers in the men’s javelin throw qualifying round at the Commonwealth Games 2026 in Glasgow, Scotland on July 30, with Arshad Nadeem ranking seventh. — screengrab via glasgow2026.com Also competing in the event was Muhammad Yasir, who threw his season’s best of 74.36m but failed to make the top 12 qualifiers, finishing in 14th place. At last year’s Asian Throwing Championships, the Yasir threw a massive 77.43m on his sixth and final attempt, snagging a bronze medal and smashing his previous season’s best. In his comments earlier this month, Arshad recalled memories of the 2022 Commonwealth Games and acknowledged the pressure he felt to live up to his accolades. “Four years after I broke the Commonwealth Games record in 2022, I remain in the same position,” the star athlete said. “There is also pressure [on me] … I have been the champion for four years and now I will need to again do well [to retain the title].” “There is always pressure while entering the field … that pressure has to be controlled.”

items.title: Azzedine Ounahi se rapproche d'un transfert à Al-Ittihad
items.description: L'avenir d'Azzedine Ounahi pourrait s'écrire en Arabie saoudite. L'international marocain est de plus en plus proche de rejoindre Al-Ittihad, alors que les négociations avec Gérone auraient considérablement progressé ces dernières heures. Selon les informations d'Africa Foot, les deux clubs sont proches d'un accord définitif. Il ne resterait plus que quelques détails à régler, principalement liés aux modalités de paiement de l'indemnité de transfert. Le média précise que Gérone souhaite percevoir le montant prévu par la clause de départ du joueur. De son côté, Al-Ittihad aurait proposé de régler cette somme en deux ou trois échéances, une formule actuellement étudiée par les dirigeants du club espagnol. Si les deux parties parviennent à s'entendre sur les conditions de paiement, le transfert d'Azzedine Ounahi vers le championnat saoudien pourrait être officialisé dans les prochains jours. Le milieu de terrain marocain sort d'une saison convaincante en Liga sous les couleurs de Gérone, avec 20 apparitions et cinq buts inscrits, confirmant son importance dans l'entrejeu du club catalan. Auteur également d'une Coupe du monde 2026 remarquée avec les Lions de l'Atlas, Ounahi continue d'attirer l'intérêt de plusieurs clubs. À ce stade, Al-Ittihad semble toutefois le mieux placé pour s'attacher ses services et pourrait bientôt accueillir le milieu marocain dans ses rangs, sous réserve d'un accord final entre les deux clubs. The post Azzedine Ounahi se rapproche d'un transfert à Al-Ittihad appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.description: BURKINA-NAMENTENGA-SPORT-JEUNESSE Namentenga : L’association Tinb Nooma boucle la première édition de son camp vacances football et reçoit les félicitations des autorités Boulsa, 30 juil. 2026 (AIB) – Le représentant du Haut-commissaire de la province du Namentenga, Batio Roger Nébié, a présidé, le samedi 25 juillet 2026 à Boulsa, la cérémonie de clôture de la première édition du camp « Top vacances football » de l’association Tinb Nooma. Il a salué l’initiative, estimant qu’elle contribue à l’éducation des enfants à travers le sport. Pendant un mois, 120 enfants âgés de 5 à 11 ans ont bénéficié d’un encadrement adapté à leur tranche d’âge afin de s’initier aux fondamentaux du football. La cérémonie de clôture a été marquée par des démonstrations des acquis des campeurs devant leurs parents et les invités. Les enfants ont exécuté des parcours techniques ainsi que des jeux individuels et collectifs, permettant au public d’apprécier les compétences acquises au cours des 30 jours de formation. Selon le président de l’association Tinb Nooma, Cydrique Korogo, cette première édition s’est déroulée dans de bonnes conditions, grâce à l’implication des encadreurs et à la confiance des parents. « Nous sommes satisfaits du déroulement du camp. L’ensemble du programme a été exécuté et aucun incident n’a été enregistré », a-t-il indiqué. M. Korogo a exprimé sa gratitude aux parents pour avoir confié leurs enfants à l’association. Il a également souhaité une mobilisation plus importante des campeurs et un accompagnement accru des partenaires pour la deuxième édition. Au nom du Haut-commissaire, Batio Roger Nébié a félicité les responsables de l’association pour leur engagement en faveur de la jeunesse. « Je vous félicite pour votre contribution à l’éducation des enfants par le sport », a-t-il déclaré, tout en encourageant les promoteurs à pérenniser cette initiative au bénéfice des enfants de la province. items.title: Balé : La commune de Fara célèbre la toute première édition de son mini marathon sous le signe de la citoyenneté et de l’engagement juvénile
items.description: Burkina/Balé-Marathon Balé : La commune de Fara célèbre la toute première édition de son mini marathon sous le signe de la citoyenneté et de l'engagement juvénile Fara, 25 juillet 2026 (AIB) – La commune de Fara a tenu sa première édition de mini marathon, le samedi 25 juillet 2026. Placée sous le haut patronage du camarade Martin BAKO, haut-commissaire de la province des balé, cette édition a connu la présence des PDS de Fara et Poura, des parrains et des invités d'honneur. Au total, 45 athlètes ont pris part dont une femme. Elle s'est déroulée sous le thème : « Sport et citoyenneté pour une jeunesse engagée ». Le lancement officiel de la compétition, les allocutions et les remises de prix ont constitué les temps forts de la cérémonie de cette activité. Le top départ de la compétition a été donné à 8 h 15 mn pour une distance de 21 km à parcourir en aller-retour. Le premier a franchi la ligne d'arrivée après une durée d'1 heure 9 mn 30 s et vient de la cité de Bankui. Un mineur de 11 ans a également participé à ce marathon. Le président du comité d'organisation a dans sa prise de parole a traduit sa reconnaissance à tous les participants et les différentes personnes qui ont soutenu la tenue de cette compétition. Le Président de la délégation spéciale (PDS) de Fara dans son discours a remercié le camarade haut-commissaire pour sa présence à cette compétition sportive. Il a traduit sa reconnaissance aux parrains et au comité d'organisation ainsi que tous les marathoniens. Il a souligné l'importance du sport et son impact pour les pratiquants. Il a en outre rappelé l'importance du thème de cette édition. Pour lui, la jeunesse doit s'engager dans la citoyenneté pour la patrie. Pour les parrains, c'est un honneur et une opportunité pour eux d'apporter leur touche à la réussite de cette activité et au-delà toutes les activités de développement de la commune. Le camarade haut-commissaire a félicité le PDS de Fara ainsi que le comité d'organisation pour la tenue effective de cette activité. Il a félicité et apprécié les athlètes pour les performances réalisées. Pour lui, la tenue de cette édition démontre la volonté de l'autorité communale à faire du sport pour tous, une initiative présidentielle une réalité dans son ressort territorial. La cérémonie s'est achevée par la remise de prix spéciaux, des prix pour les 10 premiers marathoniens. Le premier a reçu des mains du haut-commissaire, des PDS et des parrains, les clés d'une moto et un bon de carburant. Rendez-vous a été pris pour la deuxième édition. Agence d'Information du Burkina. EK-DNK

Les douze candidats présentés par le lycée ont tous été déclarés admis, confirmant ainsi les bonnes performances de cet établissement de la province du Ioba. Selon M. Ouattara, ce résultat est le fruit des efforts conjugués des enseignants, des élèves, des parents d’élèves ainsi que des partenaires de l’établissement. « Nous éprouvons un sentiment de fierté et de satisfaction. Ces résultats traduisent les sacrifices consentis par les enseignants, l’abnégation des élèves ainsi que l’accompagnement constant des parents d’élèves et de nos différents partenaires », a-t-il déclaré. Le premier responsable du lycée a adressé ses félicitations aux nouveaux bacheliers avant de saluer le professionnalisme et l’engagement de l’ensemble de son personnel. Il a également exprimé sa reconnaissance aux autorités communales, à la direction provinciale en charge de l’enseignement secondaire et au conseil de l’établissement pour leur accompagnement. Le proviseur a enfin exhorté les nouveaux bacheliers à poursuivre leurs études supérieures avec rigueur, humilité et persévérance afin de devenir des cadres compétents au service du développement du Burkina Faso. Les douze nouveaux bacheliers prennent actuellement part à l’Immersion patriotique obligatoire (IPO) à Dano. Agence d’information du Burkina CZ/SZ-DNK

items.title: Colobane : le ministère du Commerce saisit plus de 30 000 canettes de boisson BX après des alertes sur les réseaux sociaux
items.description: Le ministère sénégalais de l'Industrie et du Commerce a confirmé, dans un communiqué daté du 30 juillet 2026, avoir mené une opération de grande ampleur contre un dépôt de distribution de produits alimentaires jugés impropres à la consommation, à Colobane, dans la région de Dakar. Le ministère du Commerce et de l’Industrie indique avoir agi « à la suite d'alertes circulant sur les réseaux sociaux concernant la dangerosité présumée » de la boisson gazeuse de marque BX. C'est la Direction du Commerce intérieur (DCI) qui a été chargée de vérifier ces signalements. Selon le communiqué, dès que l'alerte est tombée, les agents de la Division de la Consommation et de la Sécurité des consommateurs ont multiplié les contrôles dans les marchés et entrepôts dakarois, jusqu'à identifier ce que le ministère qualifie de « source majeure de distribution » de marchandises non conformes. Le bilan de la saisie L'opération de Colobane a permis de retirer du circuit commercial des quantités importantes de denrées : – Boisson gazeuse BX : 1 278 packs, soit 30 672 canettes de 250 ml ; – Boisson sucrée BEST : 37 cartons, soit 888 bouteilles de 330 ml ; – Couscous DALIA : 429 cartons, soit 5 148 sachets d'1 kg ; – Ainsi que diverses autres denrées alimentaires jugées non conformes. Le ministère précise que l'ensemble de ces produits a été saisi et qu'une procédure contentieuse a été ouverte contre le commerçant mis en cause. Le ministère appelle à la vigilance Dans son communiqué, le département dirigé affirme que « la protection de la santé publique est une priorité absolue » et assure que la DCI maintient « une surveillance accrue et sans relâche » sur l'ensemble du territoire national. Le ministère adresse par ailleurs trois recommandations : faire preuve de vigilance lors de l'achat de denrées alimentaires ; vérifier systématiquement l'intégrité et les dates de péremption des produits ; signaler toute anomalie ou produit suspect via le Numéro Vert 800 80 77 77 . O.B.N

items.title: Parliament urged to enforce mineral royalty disbursements
items.description: Ghana’s Extractive Sector Multi-Stakeholder Group (MSG) has urged Parliament to summon state agencies over delays in disbursing mineral royalties to mining host communities. The group said the delays were stalling development projects, disrupting local planning, and undermining the objectives of the Minerals Development Fund Act. Dr Emmanuel Steve Asare Manteaw, a member of the MSG, made the call at a media engagement to disseminate the findings of the 2023 Ghana Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (GHEITI) Report in Accra. He attributed the persistent delays to weak oversight, saying Parliament should ensure compliance with the Minerals Development Fund Act, 2016 (Act 912), by holding state institutions accountable for the timely release of approved funds. “A lot of development projects in some of these beneficiary communities have come to a standstill, and the uncertainty over the timing of disbursements makes it difficult for communities to plan development activities with any confidence. “What is more worrying is the role of Parliament in all this because they passed the law mandating that certain percentages of mineral royalties be disbursed to mining host communities,” Dr. Manteaw said. He said Parliament should ensure that information on delayed payments, including the institutions responsible and the amounts outstanding, was made public to strengthen transparency and accountability. In a speech read on his behalf, Patrick Nomo, Co-Chair of the GHEITI Multi-Stakeholder Group and Chief Director at the Ministry of Finance, said reforms to the mineral royalty regime had improved the management of extractive revenues. He said GHEITI advocacy had contributed to reforms, including changes to the mineral royalty regime and the institutionalisation of subnational royalty transfers through the Minerals Development Fund to enable mining communities to benefit more directly from mineral resources. Mr Nomo, however, said revenue leakages and weak inter-institutional coordination continued to constrain the sector’s contribution to national and local development. He called for stronger institutional collaboration and improved data management to enhance transparency and ensure that resource revenues translated into tangible benefits for mining communities. Mr Nomo reaffirmed the government’s commitment to using evidence generated through GHEITI to inform policy reforms and strengthen accountability in the extractive sector. Under the Minerals Development Fund Act, mineral royalties are distributed through a statutory formula, with district assemblies receiving 55 percent of the allocation to local government, mining-affected communities 25 percent, and traditional councils 20 percent.

items.title: Attorney General to challenge Sedina Tamakloe acquittal at Supreme Court; files for stay of execution
items.description: The Attorney General has directed the Director of Public Prosecutions to immediately file an appeal to the Supreme Court challenging the Court of Appeal’s decision acquitting and discharging former MASLOC CEO Sedina Tamakloe Attionu. In a press release issued on July 30, 2026, the Attorney General stated that it had taken notice of the Court of Appeal’s ruling overturning the conviction of the former MASLOC boss on 78 counts, including conspiracy to steal, stealing, causing financial loss to the State, money laundering, and breaches of the Public Procurement Act. READ ALSO: Court of Appeal acquits, discharges ex-MASLOC CEO Sedina Tamakloe-Attionu “Having received notice of the Court of Appeal’s decision, the Attorney-General has directed the Director of Public Prosecutions to immediately file a notice of appeal to the Supreme Court, together with an application for a stay of execution of the judgment pending the determination of the appeal,” the statement read. The press release, dated July 30, 2026, emphasised that the state is not backing down from the case. “The Republic opposed the appeal by filing written submissions, contending that the appeal lacked merit and ought to be dismissed,” the statement added. “The Attorney-General remains committed to the due process of law and is confident that the appeal before the Supreme Court will succeed.” The Court of Appeal, in a unanimous decision earlier today, acquitted and discharged Sedina Tamakloe Attionu, who had been convicted in absentia by the High Court on April 16, 2024, and sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment with hard labour. The appellate court, presided over by Justice Emmanuel Ankamah, Justice Emmanuel Senyo Amedahe, and Justice Samuel Obeng-Diawuo, ruled that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The court also held that the trial judge lost sight of the constitutional principle that every accused person is presumed innocent until proven guilty. Lawyer for the acquitted former MASLOC CEO, Enoch Deegbe, speaking to Class News moments after the ruling, disclosed that the Court of Appeal based its decision primarily on the defective charge sheet used to prosecute his client. Deegbe said his legal team had come on three main grounds—the defective charge sheet, lack of proper prima facie determination against the client, and attacks on the judgment itself—but the court dwelt primarily on the first leg of their submission. Daniel Axim, Tamakloe’s co-accused who was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment, remains out on bail granted by the Supreme Court in January 2026 pending his own appeal. He has served nearly two years of his sentence. Following the Court of Appeal’s decision to acquit and discharge Tamakloe, and now the state’s decision to appeal that ruling, the status of Axim’s appeal and the broader implications for the case remain uncertain. items.title: Delegate system ruling won’t eradicate monetisation in party elections – Political observers
items.description: A Political Scientist and Senior Lecturer at Kumasi Technical University, Dr. Samuel Afriyie, has described the Supreme Court’s decision to declare the delegate system unconstitutional as a step in the right direction. In an interview with JoyNews, Dr. Afriyie noted that while the ruling seeks to curb money politics and widen participation in internal party elections, it is unlikely to completely eliminate monetization in political party primaries. “The Supreme Court’s decision is a good one, but it will only help reduce, not eradicate, bribery and corruption in the electoral system,” he said. Dr. Afriyie explained that monetization in party primaries has become deeply entrenched over the years. He argued that even with a broader voter base, candidates with financial muscle may still find ways to influence outcomes through gifts, logistics, and other forms of inducement. “The challenge is not just about the size of the delegates. It is about the culture of money politics that has developed within our parties,” he added. The Supreme Court has, by a 5-2 majority decision, ruled aspects of the delegate system used by political parties to elect presidential and parliamentary candidates as unconstitutional. The court ordered political parties to replace the system within one year with one that allows all members in good standing to vote. The ruling has triggered debate on reforms needed to make party primaries more transparent and participatory. But Dr. Afriyie argued that while the court’s interpretation may be well-intentioned, it does not adequately address the practical realities of implementing such a system. According to him, expanding voting rights to all party members could place enormous financial and logistical burdens on political parties’ members and aspirants. He also questioned how political parties would determine who qualifies as a member in good standing, noting that the Supreme Court’s ruling leaves that responsibility to the parties. “Now it is up to the political party to determine who its members in good standing are, and that will largely depend on the fulfillment of financial obligations. The parties may also increase dues, nomination, and filing fees for aspirants,” he said. In Kumasi, the ruling has been met with optimism. However, some residents share the political scientist’s view that it will not completely eliminate monetisation in political party primaries. They believe the ruling addresses long-standing concerns about money influencing internal party elections, as well as the gap between delegates and the wider party membership. “It will cure a certain mischief,” one resident said. “First, the monetisation of our politics, and second, the situation where the general electorate feel that delegates did not elect the candidate they wanted.” Other residents added that the decision could help restore confidence in party primaries and deepen democratic participation by granting all members in good standing the right to vote. They added that while implementation may come with challenges, broadening participation is necessary to make internal elections more credible.

items.title: Joy as Kristo Asafo Mission members celebrate Apostle Kwadwo Safo’s life at Gomoa Mpota
items.description: Members of the Kristo Asafo Mission Church gathered at Gomoa Mpota in the Central Region in a spirit of celebration to honour the life and legacy of their founder, Apostle Kwadwo Safo Kantanka. The funeral grounds were filled with songs of praise, thanksgiving and worship as church members sang and danced, expressing gratitude to God for the life and contributions of the late apostle. Rather than focusing only on grief, many members described the occasion as an opportunity to celebrate the achievements of a visionary leader whose influence went beyond the church to areas such as technology, agriculture and industrial development. Dressed in colourful church outfits, members lifted their voices in thanksgiving, praising God for the years Apostle Kwadwo Safo Kantanka spent on earth and the impact he made through his ministry and innovations. Speaking to Adom News, some church members described the funeral as a historic and emotional moment. They expressed appreciation to the leadership of the Kristo Asafo Mission and former Dome-Kwabenya Member of Parliament, Sarah Adwoa Safo, for their roles in ensuring the late founder received a befitting farewell. They said they were grateful that Apostle Kwadwo Safo Kantanka was being honoured in a manner befitting his contribution to the church, Ghanaian innovation and national development. According to them, the late apostle’s legacy would continue to inspire future generations, particularly through his commitment to self-reliance, creativity and technological advancement. The funeral attracted hundreds of mourners, including members of the Kristo Asafo Mission, traditional leaders, public figures and admirers of the renowned inventor and industrialist. Apostle Kwadwo Safo Kantanka, founder of the Kristo Asafo Mission and the Kantanka Group of Companies, was widely recognised for his pioneering work in engineering, automobile manufacturing and the promotion of local innovation. His passing has attracted tributes from across the country, with many celebrating his contributions to Ghana’s religious, technological and industrial landscape. The funeral is also being held amid a legal dispute after the Accra High Court granted a 10-day interim injunction restraining Mrs. Sarah Adwoa Safo from proceeding with the funeral arrangements. The court order was issued to preserve the status quo while the substantive issues surrounding the arrangements are determined. Despite the injunction, mourners have continued to throng Gomoa Mpota, with funeral activities and tributes ongoing.

items.title: Court grants Hanan permission to leave proceedings on medical grounds
items.description: The Accra High Court (Specialised Court 1) today granted permission to the first accused in the National Food Buffer Stock Company (NAFCO) case, Hanan Abdul-Wahab Aludiba, to excuse himself from the remainder of the day’s proceedings after considering a medical excuse presented to the court. In its ruling, the court stated that although the excuse duty did not specify the specific ailments for Hanan Abdul-Wahab, it had no reason to doubt its authenticity, though the A-G strongly opposed this. The court further noted that Hanan had personally appeared before it to seek leave to absent himself in accordance with the excuse duty. The presiding judge therefore granted the application, observing that Hanan Abdul-Wahab should be allowed to take his medication and obtain the rest he indicated he required. The court ordered that Hanan Abdul-Wahab be at liberty to excuse himself from the proceedings if he so desired. It further directed that the trial would continue in his absence, having regard to the nature of the business before the court. Immediately after the ruling was delivered, Hanan Abdul-Wahab walked out of the courtroom in accordance with the court’s permission, while proceedings continued with the remaining parties. The court is currently hearing the motion for a stay of proceedings by Hanan’s lawyers.

items.title: La Tunisie s’active, sous pression, à réformer son réseau électrique
items.description: Ce n’est pas la solution miracle au déficit énergétique de la Tunisie, dont le taux dépasse aujourd’hui 60%, mais c’est une solution temporaire qui peut aider le pays à dépasser la crise qu’il traverse depuis deux semaines, marquée par des coupures intempestives d’électricité dues à la forte hausse de la demande dans un contexte de canicule estivale. Solutions temporaires en attendant l’entrée en production des nombreuses centrales solaires photovoltaïques en cours de construction. La Société tunisienne de l’électricité et du gaz (Steg) vient d’annoncer la mise en service d’un transformateur de 360 ​​mégavolt-ampères (MVA) au poste à haute tension de Mornaguia, un nœud majeur du réseau alimentant l’agglomération de Tunis, ainsi que l’arrivée imminente d’une seconde unité de 400 MVA. Ces deux équipements fabriqués en Chine permettront d’accroître la capacité du réseau national de transport. Et d’améliorer la stabilité de l’approvisionnement en électricité. Bien que la mise en service du premier transformateur constitue une avancée, les experts estiment que cette infrastructure aurait dû être achevée dès 2020. Ce retard de plusieurs années illustre les difficultés rencontrées pour investir dans la modernisation du réseau national. Renforcer la résilience du réseau de la Steg durant les mois d’été Ce projet est désormais complété par un second transformateur de 400 MVA, qui accroîtra encore la capacité de transport d’électricité et réduira les risques de congestion lors des pics de demande. L’objectif de la Steg est de renforcer la résilience du réseau, en particulier durant les mois d’été, période où l’utilisation généralisée de la climatisation porte la consommation d’électricité à ses niveaux les plus élevés de l’année. Sur le plan technique, un transformateur de ce type ne produit pas d’énergie, mais il joue un rôle essentiel dans le réseau de transport : il transforme les niveaux de tension entre les différentes sections du réseau électrique, augmentant ainsi la capacité de transport d’énergie et réduisant les pertes. Une disponibilité accrue de puissance aux nœuds stratégiques permet également le raccordement de nouvelles centrales de production et une distribution plus efficace de l’électricité vers les centres de consommation. Toutefois, les récentes coupures d’électricité enregistrées dans plusieurs régions du pays ne sont pas uniquement dues à des défaillances techniques ; elles reflètent une gestion planifiée du réseau visant à éviter un effondrement lors des pics de consommation. Ces dernières semaines, la Steg a procédé à des coupures temporaires d’électricité dans de nombreuses zones du Grand Tunis et dans d’autres gouvernorats, alors que les températures atteignaient 50 degrés Celsius, alimentant ainsi la controverse sur la capacité du système à répondre à une demande croissante. La modernisation du réseau revêt également une importance stratégique dans le contexte de la transition énergétique de la Tunisie. Le pays accélère le développement de nouveaux parcs photovoltaïques et éoliens et vise à accroître considérablement la part des énergies renouvelables dans son mix énergétique. L’augmentation de la production issue de sources intermittentes nécessite un réseau de transport plus robuste et plus flexible, capable d’absorber et de distribuer des volumes d’électricité plus importants. Le renforcement des infrastructures électriques est également étroitement lié aux grands projets d’interconnexion internationale, notamment le câble sous-marin Elmed, qui reliera la Tunisie à l’Italie via la Sicile. L’augmentation de la capacité du réseau national est une condition nécessaire pour que le pays puisse tirer parti des futures exportations d’énergie et s’intégrer progressivement au marché de l’électricité euro-méditerranéen. Toutefois, la question des investissements requis pour rattraper des années de retard dans la maintenance et la modernisation des infrastructures reste en suspens. L’arrivée des deux transformateurs constitue un signe concret de renforcement du réseau, mais les experts s’accordent à dire qu’un programme plus vaste d’interventions sur les lignes à haute tension, les postes électriques et les capacités de production sera nécessaire pour garantir la sécurité énergétique de la Tunisie dans les années à venir. Améliorer la performance et la gouvernance de la Steg Le 14 juillet, le Parlement a approuvé deux projets de loi autorisant des accords de garantie de l’État pour des prêts accordés par la Banque mondiale à la Steg, destinés à financer le programme d’amélioration de l’efficacité et de la gouvernance du secteur énergétique. Les deux accords ont été signés le 3 novembre 2025, et l’examen parlementaire a débuté le 10 juillet. Le premier concerne un prêt de 384,8 millions d’euros (environ 1,3 milliard de dinars tunisiens) accordé à la Steg pour soutenir le programme de réforme du secteur de l’énergie. Le projet de loi a été adopté par 72 voix pour, 6 abstentions et 19 voix contre. Ce prêt, d’une durée de 43 ans incluant une période de grâce de sept ans, prévoit, outre les investissements, une série de réformes structurelles, telles que la création d’une autorité de régulation du secteur de l’énergie, l’adoption des normes internationales d’information financière (IFRS) par la Steg et le renforcement du recouvrement des créances. Le second projet de loi autorise une garantie de l’État pour un prêt de 30 millions de dollars (environ 25,7 millions d’euros) accordé par la Banque internationale pour la reconstruction et le développement (Bird), agissant en tant qu’organisme d’exécution du Fonds pour les technologies propres ; ce prêt vise également à financer le programme d’amélioration de la performance et de la gouvernance de la Steg. Lors d’une récente réunion au ministère de l’Industrie, des Mines et de l’Énergie à Tunis avec des représentants du secteur, plusieurs propositions ont été présentées, notamment l’intégration de transformateurs hybrides et de systèmes de stockage par batterie, le déploiement de compteurs intelligents, la simplification des procédures administratives, l’introduction de nouvelles mesures incitatives et d’allégements fiscaux, ainsi que la mise à jour du cadre réglementaire pour encourager les investissements dans la production d’électricité à partir de sources renouvelables. Le ministre Salah Zouari a rappelé que «la STEG a récemment publié un document technique réglementant l’installation, par les clients résidentiels, de batteries associées à des transformateurs hybrides pour les systèmes photovoltaïques, une initiative préparée ces derniers mois pour encourager le développement de l’autoconsommation énergétique» . La Tunisie vise à porter la part des énergies renouvelables dans la production d’électricité à 35 % d’ici 2030 et à 50 % d’ici 2035 — contre 9 % actuellement — grâce à l’installation d’une capacité éolienne et solaire de 5 000 mégawatts. Selon des données récemment publiées par le ministère, l’État consacre chaque année plus de trois milliards de dinars (environ 900 millions d’euros) en subventions pour couvrir une partie des coûts de production d’électricité, alors que le pays continue d’importer environ 80 % de ses besoins en gaz naturel et 10 % de sa consommation d’électricité, malgré un taux d’électrification atteignant 99 % de la population. Le programme de réforme de la Steg, prévu jusqu’en 2028, comprend le rééquilibrage financier de l’entreprise, l’amélioration de l’efficacité commerciale et technique, le recouvrement des créances et le renforcement de la gouvernance. Parmi les projets majeurs figurent la construction d’un corridor électrique entre le nord et le sud de la Tunisie pour favoriser l’intégration des énergies renouvelables au réseau national, la modernisation des infrastructures de distribution, l’installation de 150 000 compteurs intelligents lors de la phase initiale et l’amélioration de la qualité du service. L’article La Tunisie s’active, sous pression, à réformer son réseau électrique est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Cracks in the Universal Health Insurance system: An accounting of phase 1
items.description: In the government’s telling, the first phase of the Universal Health Insurance rollout was a success . And with that success in hand, it says now that the scheme is ready to expand. Six years ago, people in Port Said, Ismailia, Suez, South Sinai, Luxor and Aswan — the first governorates to see the rollout of the 2018 law — were brought into the new system. The promise was something better than the old model, a healthcare system built on social solidarity. People would pay less out of pocket. They would find a place in hospitals. Medicines and treatment would be there when they needed them. But patients across those six governorates who spoke to Mada Masr over recent months describe months-long shortages of critical medicines and medical devices and appointment scheduling bottlenecks. Many, who were enrolled in the program whether they wanted to join or not, are now being effectively denied healthcare over unpaid insurance contributions that have climbed in some cases into the tens of thousands of pounds. “All we hear is that the system is a success, but what we see is something completely different,” says a resident of Aswan. What is on the ground is a service well below even the minimum standard, he says. The problems in the first phase were not unforeseen. Several officials and health policy experts involved in the drafting of the law at the time tell Mada Masr that the objections they raised nearly a decade ago remain at the heart of the challenges patients face today. Nonetheless, the government is pressing ahead. While Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar says the government is preparing amendments to the law to address shortcomings that emerged during implementation, the state is already heavily promoting the second phase that will expand the scheme to another five governorates, starting with Minya, a heavily populated governorate with one of the highest poverty rates in the country. Mada Masr spoke with health sector officials, specialist researchers, MPs and beneficiaries of the system to examine the main crises and challenges that emerged during the first phase, and whether they are now being carried into the scheme’s expansion. *** One of the most common complaints patients living in the first-phase governorates raise is the shortage of medication. For Mohamed Yasser, from Port Said, it was Budelizer, an inhaled medication used to treat asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. When his monthly prescription ran out, he was told the drug was unavailable through the scheme. It stayed that way for nearly six months. During that time, Yasser had to buy the medication himself from private pharmacies, where the two boxes he needs each month cost around LE500 — even as he continued paying more than LE400 a month into the insurance scheme. Sometimes, he says, he could not find the medication or a substitute. Getting medication through the system is itself consuming, Yasser explains. Patients must first book an appointment through the call center, then wait in a long queue at a family medicine clinic for a doctor to renew the prescription, before heading to the pharmacy, then to the cashier for the required fees and finally back to pick up the medication. Every time, Yasser has to repeat the same process, which takes long hours, even though he is not seeking a medical examination but just renewing a prescription he takes regularly. Sometimes, there are no appointments available, and he is told to come back the following week, by which point he has already run out of the medicine. Other times, the doctor prescribes three packs, but the pharmacy dispenses only one because supplies are running low, forcing him to cut his dosage. Because he kept having to cut back on the medication, his condition deteriorated, he says. Eventually, he filed a complaint with the Universal Health Insurance Authority demanding that the medication be made available again, noting that it had previously been dispensed routinely through the system before suddenly disappearing. Khaled, an Al-Azhar school teacher in his mid-forties who lives in the Aboul Rish neighborhood in Aswan, has run into the same problem. He depends on regular insulin injections and diabetes medication. Yet attempts to obtain them through his designated insurance hospital have repeatedly failed. “They told me, ‘buy it from outside, when you get paid,’” he tells Mada Masr. Despite around LE800 being deducted from his salary every month in insurance contributions, he recently had to cover all of his treatment costs out of pocket. “I bought the insulin, eye drops, and also some vitamins, because none of them were available.” Whenever Ahmed Yehia, an accountant from Luxor, accompanies his mother to collect her medication, they often leave empty-handed or with only part of the prescription, forcing him to buy the missing medicines from private pharmacies. One of the drugs she regularly cannot obtain is Diamicron 60, used to treat type 2 diabetes. The two boxes she needs each month cost almost as much as the LE500 deducted from Yehia’s income in monthly insurance contributions. He questions the point of paying into the insurance system if that is the case. “We are paying for nothing and getting no service,” he says. Patients speaking to Mada Masr say access breaks down at almost every stage of the system. Even securing an appointment can take weeks, sometimes months. In May, Khaled, the school teacher from Aswan, visited his insurance dental clinic while suffering from severe tooth pain. After waiting for hours to be seen, he was told to return two months later because the clinic “doesn’t have the specialist equipment.” With no other option, he paid LE1,400 for treatment at a private clinic. Others describe the same pattern of delays. Mostafa, from Port Said, says he spent weeks trying to book a dental appointment. Every time he called, he was told there were no available slots. “I know people who book an appointment every week just in case they get sick. That’s an odd thing to do,” he says. “I’ve been trying for three weeks. Every time I go, they tell me the system is down.” At one point he asked for doctors to just prescribe medication instead of an appointment. “What can I do?” the staff replied, “The system is down.” “All we hear is that the system is a success, but what we see is something completely different,” Khaled tells Mada Masr. The long waits for appointments, poor patient care from doctors and shortages of medicines and basic medical supplies all point to a service still well below even the minimum standard, he says. For infants and young children who depend on specialist treatment, blocking access to medications carries a much higher risk. Under the Universal Health Insurance system, families seeking insulin pumps, continuous glucose monitors or other high-cost treatments for their children are required to first obtain a court order. Even then, access is not guaranteed. Some have responded by taking the authority itself to court. Ahmed Ibrahim, the father of Aisha, who filed a case before a Port Said administrative court seeking to compel the Universal Health Insurance Authority to provide Naglazyme, an enzyme replacement therapy. The authority had refused to cover the treatment despite his daughter’s diagnosis with mucopolysaccharidosis VI (MPS VI), or Maroteaux–Lamy syndrome , a rare sugar metabolic disorder, and medical reports issued by the Mansoura University Children’s Hospital and Egypt Healthcare Authority confirming that she needs it. In a report on the case, a copy of which Mada Masr obtained, the State Commissioners Authority recommended that prior to the court issuing a final ruling, the Egyptian Forensic Medicine Authority must examine Aisha, determine whether the treatment is medically necessary and assess the appropriate dosage. The report cites Article 18 of the Constitution and the 2018 Universal Health Insurance Law, both of which guarantee the right to healthcare and require the authority to finance treatment for insured patients. It also refers to established Supreme Administrative Court rulings holding that a public authority’s failure to take a decision required by law constitutes a negative administrative decision that can be challenged before the courts. If medical necessity is established, the report concludes, the authority cannot justify withholding treatment simply because it falls outside its dispensing protocols. The constitutional and legal obligation to protect the rights to health and life, it says, takes precedence over administrative restrictions. Pending the forensic assessment, it provisionally recommended that the court overturn the authority’s refusal and require it to provide treatment. Ahmed al-Desouky, another Port Said resident, filed a similar case in an effort to secure continued coverage for his nine-year-old daughter Mariam, who has lived with dermatomyositis, an autoimmune disease affecting the skin and muscles, for the past two and a half years. Her case is due to be heard on August 28. Desouky says Mariam depends on intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG) infusions, a concentrated mix of antibodies, and Xeljanz, an enzyme inhibitor. In 2019, a course of the IVIG treatment cost LE18,000. She continued receiving the medication through the old health insurance system until Universal Health Insurance fully replaced it in 2021. Today, he says, the treatment is theoretically dispensed every month. In practice, he is often told that the medication is unavailable within the system or that there is nowhere to obtain it. Repeated delays in receiving the medications have caused his daughter’s condition to worsen. Lesions have spread across her body, and she is losing the ability to walk, he says. Cases like Aisha’s and Mariam’s are emblematic of the system failures criticized in four parliamentary briefing requests MP Ahmed Farghaly submitted in April over the implementation of the Universal Health Insurance scheme in Port Said. Addressed to the health and finance ministers and the head of the authority responsible for financing the system, the requests accuse the authority of treating healthcare as a commercial commodity, prioritizing costs over patient needs. For Farghaly, children are among those paying the highest price. Under the previous system, he said, insulin pumps and glucose monitoring devices for newborns and children with diabetes were provided according to medical criteria. Under the Universal Health Insurance system, they are limited to families who obtain court orders or children already using the devices before the new scheme was introduced in their governorates. Some families have already secured court rulings ordering the authority to provide them, yet the rulings have gone unenforced, according to Farghaly. Children who are too young to recognize or communicate the symptoms of high blood sugar face severe health risks without the devices, he said. The devices would cost the state only a few thousand pounds a month, Farghaly argued, while denying them can leave children in intensive care, ultimately driving up treatment costs for the state. Farghaly said that the same logic extends beyond pediatric care. He accused the authority of replacing Prograf, the original immunosuppressant prescribed to kidney transplant patients, with the cheaper alternative Adport. Around 150 transplant patients have been “neglected” as a result, he said. Having undergone cycles of dialysis and transplants in the hope of returning to normal lives, they were switched from Prograf to Adport several months prior, a change that, he said, has caused complications in some cases and left several patients hospitalized despite repeated warnings that the switch posed “a threat to their lives.” His briefing requests also pointed to shortages in dialysis capacity. According to Farghaly, dozens of patients who require dialysis three times a week have been referred to private hospitals because insurance hospitals lack capacity. But under their contracts with the authority, private hospitals only provide dialysis sessions, leaving patients to pay out of pocket for medicines, follow-up tests and even blood transfusions when needed. A former senior official at the health insurance authority says that telling a patient to “come back at the end of the month” just to book an appointment is “nonsense,” adding: “The maximum wait should be a week. If you’re telling patients to come back at the end of the month, then it means you don’t have enough doctors. And if there is a shortage of doctors, then that’s a big problem.” Right to Medicine Foundation head Mahmoud Fouad questions the logic of charging such high insurance contributions under the scheme while failing to provide the promised services. “You can’t tell patients there is no medicine available when they are obliged to pay into the system,” he says. “If I’m using the service, I’m supposed to find it. It is not right that I receive only part of it.” *** For some patients, the barrier begins before they see a doctor, before they pick up a prescription and before the system provides any care at all. It begins with a debt. Five patients tell Mada Masr they discovered they have accumulated insurance contribution arrears only when they tried to access treatment. They all share one thing in common: unlike employees whose contributions are deducted automatically by their employers, they are personally responsible for paying their insurance contributions. Mohamed, a grocery store worker in his mid-forties from Luxor and a father of two, enrolled in the Universal Health Insurance scheme in 2021 and received his insurance card, but he never used it. Six months ago, he developed rheumatoid arthritis. As the pain worsened, he went to Luxor International Hospital, part of the Universal Health Insurance system, hoping to receive a biologic injection used to treat inflammatory arthritis — which costs around LE15,000 outside the scheme. Instead, he says, he was told he owed the insurance system LE35,000. “I was shocked. I don’t know what it’s for,” Mohamed tells Mada Masr. “I’ve never had a single examination. I activated the card and put it away. Suddenly, I owe money to the healthcare system that is supposed to be treating me.” He then turned to the state’s Hayah Karima initiative for supporting people living in rural areas, hoping it could help cover the treatment. Instead, he was told he first needed to obtain a social insurance status printout. But securing that document requires him to clear the outstanding debts on his Universal Health Insurance account. For now, Mohamed is surviving on painkillers, he says. “The pain is so severe, it’s unbearable. Even at my job in the grocery store, there are products I can’t lift anymore. Biologic therapy is the only solution.” But with his outstanding insurance debts, it remains out of reach. Patients who cannot afford their contributions are meant to receive state support. According to Fouad, the Social Solidarity Ministry and the Universal Health Insurance Authority have signed a protocol to fund healthcare for people unable to pay. But what that support covers remains unclear. The agreement does not specify how much funding is available, Fouad said, or even whether it only covers medical examinations or extends to treatment itself. MPs have also questioned the scope of the funding, he added. To qualify, patients are required to obtain a “poverty certificate” proving financial hardship from the Social Solidarity Ministry before navigating a lengthy bureaucratic process involving multiple government offices, after which they are informed whether they qualify for assistance. Yehia, the accountant from Luxor who works without a contract, has also run into a dead end. He owes around LE18,000 in Universal Health Insurance arrears. But attempts to resolve the issue have stalled because he has been told he must first obtain an insurance status printout from the social insurance authority, where he also has outstanding contributions, bringing what he owes the state to around LE40,000. Cases like Mohamed’s and Yehia’s have become increasingly common over the past year, according to Mohamed Hassan Khalil, the coordinator of the Committee for the Defense of the Right to Health. Patients who seek treatment, he says, are instead confronted with insurance debts that can reach tens of thousands of pounds. Rather than functioning as social health insurance, he argues, what is in place now is essentially a low-grade, compulsory commercial insurance scheme, where keeping up with payments becomes a condition for accessing care. A former health insurance official who also served on the committee that drafted the Universal Health Insurance Law says the problem lies less with compulsory enrollment itself than how it is being implemented. People who have not used the service for years can find themselves confronted with large accumulated debts the moment they seek treatment, debts they were not aware were building up. They are only told about them once medical care becomes unavoidable, the former official explains. Responding to questions about the growing contribution arrears, Health Ministry spokesperson Hossam Abdel Ghaffar tells Mada Masr that many people simply failed to register when they were supposed to. “Out of consideration for the citizens’ circumstances, we have allowed installment plans, and we haven’t denied treatment even if someone owes money,” Abdel Ghaffar says. “Even so, there was not much interest, despite the fact that they can spread payments over several years. Even paying a single installment would show good faith.” At the end of the day, he says, the system needs a sustainable funding mechanism. Frustration with the scheme has driven many people to look for ways to avoid it altogether, after finding themselves required to pay monthly contributions without receiving the medicines or services they expected, Mohamed Senan from Qena says. Some of Senan’s relatives and friends in Luxor have changed the addresses on their ID cards. By signing new rental contracts, they were able to register as residents of governorates where the insurance system has yet to be rolled out. “We get nothing from the new system except deductions [from our income],” Senan says, arguing that the quality of care has not improved compared with the old health insurance system. Mostafa, a 40-year-old father from Ismailia with muscular dystrophy, says he considered doing the same. He looked into changing his registered address to Sharqiya to leave the scheme. But he found that doing so required a registered rental contract and complicated administrative procedures. “I found it too difficult. It didn’t work,” he says. Mostafa had gone to Salam hospital seeking an exemption from the LE250 monthly insurance contribution, explaining that his condition makes him unable to work. “I was supposed to go get my insurance card. But instead they told me I owed LE11,000,” he says. “I asked, ‘What is that for?’ They said that once Universal Health Insurance started in the governorate, anyone whose ID says Ismailia was automatically enrolled.” Hospital staff told him the system relies on civil registry records to determine who falls under the scheme. “Why doesn’t anyone tell us we have to pay so we can avoid accumulating debt?” Mostafa asks. Despite being unemployed due to his condition, staff told him that the minimum contribution is LE250, even for people without jobs. He showed them his integrated services card, a document issued by the Social Solidarity Ministry to people with disabilities. “They told me, ‘We don’t recognize that,’” he says. “How can the health insurance system not recognize a disability?” They told Mostafa he needs to be enrolled in the Takaful and Karama program. “I’ve been trying to get onto it, but I still can’t,” he says. *** Over the previous four decades, the public health insurance system expanded through a series of laws that extended coverage to different groups, repeatedly adjusting how the system was financed. In 1964, the state established the country’s first national health insurance system. Law 75 covered government employees and Law 63 covered workers in public and private sectors insured under the Social Insurance Law. The two laws established the basic model of employer-to-employee contributions. Another overhaul followed in 1975 with the passage of two laws that remain in force today. Law 32 reduced contribution rates for government employees and the government as the employer, but introduced payments that insured patients would pay when receiving healthcare services. Law 79 maintained higher contribution rates for public enterprise and formal private-sector workers, without introducing the patient co-payments found in Law 32. These differing arrangements reflected attempts to cope with the successive financial crises facing the health insurance system rather than a coherent strategy, health policy researchers Alaa Ghannam and Ahmed Azab tell Mada Masr. As Egypt entered its open-door policy era, the healthcare system came under increasing strain. Out-of-pocket spending on medical care and medicines continued to rise, while public spending on health steadily declined, pushing large segments of the population, particularly poorer, marginalized and informally employed Egyptians, outside the reach of the public healthcare system, according to an article by Azab and Ghannam. By the mid-1990s, policymakers had begun openly discussing comprehensive reform. And over the following decade, successive governments drafted new health insurance legislation, but none became law. After the 2011 revolution, the draft law was extensively revised. The process gained new momentum following the adoption of the 2014 Constitution, which committed the state to establishing a comprehensive health insurance system. A committee bringing together government officials, health policy experts and civil society groups spent the following years debating and revising the draft, presenting it across numerous sessions to the National Social Dialogue before completing its work in 2016. In 2017, the Health Ministry, whose head chaired the committee, submitted the Universal Health Insurance bill to Parliament. While previous attempts had dragged on for decades, the final push moved with speed. The bill was passed in 2018 and signed into law by the president. The law was intended to resolve many of the structural problems by replacing the patchwork of insurance schemes with a unified national system, covering all Egyptian citizens residing in the country. The law envisions a gradual nationwide rollout over 13 years, divided into six geographical phases. Unlike the previous health insurance system, which covered specific categories of formal-sector workers, the Universal Health Insurance scheme is financed through mandatory contributions paid by all citizens. The contributions are deducted directly from incomes in a system akin to taxation. Employees continue to contribute one percent of their salary, as was the case before, but the new law also requires an additional three percent for a spouse and one percent for each child. Landowners, business owners and self-employed professionals pay five percent of either their insured income or their taxable income, whichever is higher. Access to healthcare under the scheme is contingent on remaining up to date with contributions. Those who fall behind on payments must settle their arrears — either in full or through installments — before they can access services, except in emergency cases. On paper, the system represented a fundamental redesign of how healthcare would be financed and delivered. But according to people involved in drafting the law, the first phase began before many of its basic requirements were in place. Ahead of the launch in Port Said in 2019, then-Health Minister Ahmed Emad and the head of the health insurance authority at the time, Ali Hegazy, publicly maintained that everything was ready for implementation. But once it began, it quickly became clear that key elements were missing, including healthcare infrastructure and sufficient medical staff. Fouad says that during parliamentary debates over the bill, Hegazy presented “inaccurate” figures on the number of hospitals and expected beneficiaries in the first-phase governorates. Mohamed al-Ammary, then-chair of Parliament’s Health Committee, challenged those figures, saying they did not match data his committee had received from the Health Ministry and required further verification. The discrepancies ultimately led to the dismissal of Hegazy and Ammary from their posts, says Ghannam, who served on the committee that drafted the law. The former senior official, a fellow committee member, says they opposed creating an entirely new health insurance system from the outset. “I believed the old system needed reform, including for its funding resources, but, instead, they decided to build a completely new system,” they say. “That’s already a very difficult undertaking.” Fixing the flaws in the existing system and improving the quality of healthcare would have been far less costly, they argue. They say they raised these concerns before the law was passed, including in a meeting with Ammary . “My objections were clear. The priority should have been the segments most in need — women breadwinners and informal workers. You have 20 million people who need meaningful services and improved budget and contribution sources.” In their view, the old system’s biggest weakness was its financing. “In 2014, for example, total funding was around LE5 billion, and it covered more than 50 million people. Each citizen was contributing LE100 a year. That’s a very small amount. The state doesn’t finance health insurance. It is financed through contributions. So if the average is only LE100, of course there will be gaps in services.” While the new scheme appears designed to address underfunding by pooling mandatory contributions from a much broader share of the population, it does so by shifting more of the burden onto citizens. Khalil, the coordinator of the Committee for the Defense of the Right to Health, argues that the shift is part of the state’s gradual retreat from its role in financing healthcare. Under the new system, healthcare is treated as a paid service rather than a right guaranteed by the state, he says. As a result, access to care becomes tied to people’s ability to pay rather than membership in a solidarity-based society that is supposed to protect everyone, Khalil adds. He also notes that so far, the public has no visibility into how the system’s finances are managed, although the law requires its budget to be presented to Parliament and published, thereby allowing for an understanding of the size of the financial surplus and how it is being used. Ghannam agrees that the previous insurance system had become unsustainable after decades of limited coverage, low contributions and deteriorating services. It also lacked proper governance, he says, because the same institution both delivered healthcare and monitored its own performance. Many insured Egyptians avoided using it altogether, opting instead to pay private providers, he adds. But unlike the former official, Ghannam believes the idea of a universal health insurance system is sound in principle. In his view, the problem lies in how it has been implemented. A nationwide reform on this scale should have begun with a comprehensive implementation plan, Ghannam says. Instead, he argues, the rollout started before such a plan existed, without adequate infrastructure or sufficient resources, because there was political pressure to produce an “achievement.” This should have never happened, particularly given that those resources are ultimately being collected from citizens themselves, he adds. *** At a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbuly in May, the government said it is working on amendments to the 2018 law intended to overhaul the scheme’s governance, improve coordination between its bodies, strengthen its financial resources and address shortcomings that have emerged during implementation. Yet officials presented those changes as refinements to what they say was otherwise a successful first phase. Ehab Abu Eish, the deputy chair of the Universal Health Insurance Authority, said during the meeting that the scheme has so far enrolled around 5.4 million beneficiaries across the six governorates where it has been introduced, representing 83.6 percent of the target population. Around 16 percent of those enrolled are classified as unable to pay, he said at the time, describing this as evidence of the scheme’s social and humanitarian role in providing healthcare to those who need it the most. Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said in June that around 82 percent of beneficiaries are “satisfied with the services” they receive, which he described as consistent with international benchmarks. According to Fouad, there is a lot of hype surrounding the scheme. “Officials keep citing figures — 35 million services in Ismailia, 35 million services in Aswan.” He argues that officials often inflate those figures by counting administrative procedures as healthcare services. They consider registering online or giving someone a service number to be a “service” in itself, he says. “If I go to see a specialist and they refer me to a consultant, that is considered a service. And that is just marketing.” What really matters, he stresses, “is whether we get treatment, and all the treatment we need, or not.” The experiences of patients who spoke to Mada Masr across the first-phase governorates and the information and figures cited in Farghaly’s briefing requests show that the answer for many remains: no, compulsory enrollment has not translated into guaranteed treatment. The government nevertheless is moving ahead. Madbuly confirmed the government is now preparing for the second phase, which will extend the scheme to Minya, Damietta, North Sinai and Kafr al-Sheikh, adding around 12 million people to the system. Last year, the government even considered adding Alexandria to the second phase, despite having yet to present Parliament with “an accounting of the first phase,” Fouad told Mada Masr at the time. Ghannam hopes the problems that plagued the launch in Port Said will not be repeated as the second phase begins in Minya, the first governorate in the new rollout. Repeating the same mistakes there would carry far greater consequences because of Minya’s much larger population. Minya also has one of the highest rates of poverty across Egypt’s governorates, meaning the state treasury will have to shoulder a greater share of the cost of covering low-income residents, he says. Its predominantly rural population also makes the readiness of primary healthcare units and the availability of family physicians especially important. For Ghannam, Minya may prove the scheme’s first real test. But bigger challenges lie ahead. “What happens when all 100 million Egyptians are brought into the system?” the former official asks. “What will it look like then?” The post Cracks in the Universal Health Insurance system: An accounting of phase 1 first appeared on Mada Masr .

items.title: Mauritanie: plus de 240 signataires réclament une révision de la Constitution en faveur des Haratines
items.description: En Mauritanie, plus de 240 personnes ont signé une pétition pour demander la révision de la Constitution. Ils espèrent à travers cette révision une reconnaissance des Haratines comme une composante nationale et une garantie pour leurs droits politiques, économiques et culturels. Descendants d’esclaves, les Haratines sont très souvent victimes de discrimination en Mauritanie.

items.title: Algérie – Chine : forte hausse des échanges commerciaux à 9 milliards $ en six mois
items.description: Alors qu'ils étaient de 15 milliards de dollars pendant toute l’année 2025, les échanges commerciaux entre l'Algérie et la Chine se sont élevés à 9 milliards de dollars pendant les six premiers mois de 2026, en hausse de 28,3 % par rapport à la même période de l’année passée. Ces chiffres ont été révélés par l'ambassadeur de Chine en Algérie, Dong Guang Li, mercredi à l’occasion d’une rencontre à Alger dédiée à la promotion de la 140e foire de Canton. La rencontre est organisée par l’ambassade de Chine, le China foreign trade center et la Chambre algérienne de commerce et d’industrie (CACI). Les exportations de l’Algérie vers la Chine en forte hausse Suivant les chiffres fournis, les échanges sont largement à l’avantage de la Chine qui est le premier fournisseur de l’Algérie depuis 2013 au détriment de la France . Néanmoins, les exportations de l'Algérie vers ce pays sont en très forte progression. Selon Dong Guang Li, elles ont atteint 980 millions de dollars au premier semestre 2026, soit une progression de 111,6 % par rapport à la même période de 2025. Les exportations algériennes vers la Chine devraient croître davantage à la faveur de l’entrée en vigueur, le 1er mai dernier, de la franchise douanière accordée par la Chine aux produits en provenance des 53 pays d’Afrique, dont l’Algérie. La franchise douanière chinoise, une aubaine pour les produits algériens L’ambassadeur de Chine a expliqué que cette franchise “ tarif douanier zéro ” est de nature à faciliter l’accès au marché chinois de nombreux produits algériens, citant les dattes, l’huile d’olive, les agrumes… La Foire de Canton, prévue du 15 octobre au 4 novembre prochains, est aussi une opportunité pour les opérateurs algériens pour nouer des partenariats et promouvoir leurs produits, a souligné pour sa part le vice-président de la CACI, Lakhdar Madjen. Parallèlement à la hausse des échanges commerciaux entre les deux pays, la Chine compte parmi les plus importants investisseurs étrangers en Algérie avec des investissements cumulés de 7 milliards de dollars, a fait savoir M. Guang Li. L’article Algérie – Chine : forte hausse des échanges commerciaux à 9 milliards $ en six mois est apparu en premier sur TSA .
